facts.title: Street Fighting Man (1968) - Radio Resistance
facts.body: There was significant resistance to playing "Street Fighting Man" on the radio in the United States upon its release. Music critic Ralph Gleason commented on the song's "note of desperation" that appealed to "hardcore street revolutionaries." "There was also a lot of resistance to playing Street Fighting Man on the radio in the United States."

"justo al inicio de 1968 fue cuando Kate Riches, Lerroso, no viabraya, y Jones, lo que generó aparte de una enorme pelea entre ellos."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan

facts.title: Jimmy Miller's Collaboration Period (1968-1973)
facts.body: Jimmy Miller's period of collaboration with The Rolling Stones began during a low point for the band, characterized by internal strife between members like Richards and Jones, and a dip in popularity. This partnership continued until 1973, defining what would become known as The Rolling Stones' "golden age." "empieza una nueva etapa que sería la etapa durada de los Rolling Stones hasta precisamente en 1973 cuando Jimmy Miller acaba su trabajo de colaboración con los Rolling Stones."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan

facts.title: Pre-Golden Age Low Point (before 1968)
facts.body: Immediately preceding their golden age, the Rolling Stones experienced a period of significant decline, hitting rock bottom just before 1968. This was one of the lowest points in their career, even though the members were still relatively young. "justo antes del 68, cuando empezaba esa gran época, venía una pequeña época en que los Rolling Stones habían tocado fondo."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan

facts.title: Street Fighting Man (1968) - Radio Resistance
facts.body: There was significant resistance to playing "Street Fighting Man" on the radio in the United States upon its release. Music critic Ralph Gleason commented on the song's "note of desperation" that appealed to "hardcore street revolutionaries." "There was also a lot of resistance to playing Street Fighting Man on the radio in the United States."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s

facts.name: The Rolling Stones

facts.title: Street Fighting Man (1968) - Rare US Single Sleeve
facts.body: The US single for "Street Fighting Man" featured a unique sleeve with a photo of police officers beating a protester. This sleeve is exceptionally rare, with fewer than 20 copies believed to exist, because it was quickly pulled from stores. Finding one today could cost an estimated $80,000 to $90,000 or more. "Now on the sleeve, you can see there's a photo of police officers beating a protester and this sleeve is rare. I mean really rare. Like maybe less than 20 exist because it was pulled from stores pretty quickly."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s

facts.title: Time Magazine Cover (1968)
facts.body: By 1968, Aretha Franklin's cultural impact was undeniable, leading to her being featured on the cover of Time Magazine. The headline, "The Sound of Soul," underscored her widely accepted status as the ruler of soul music and a symbol of Black America. "By 1968, Franklin was on the cover of Time Magazine under the headline The Sound of Soul."

facts.title: Southern Christian Leadership Conference Award (1968)
facts.body: Aretha Franklin was honored by her friend Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. with a Southern Christian Leadership Conference Award two months before his assassination. This award acknowledged her status as a black icon and a symbol of increased confidence and pride within the African American community during the civil rights movement. "Many also saw her as a symbol of black America itself, reflecting the increased confidence and pride of African Americans in the decade of the civil rights movement and other triumphs for the black community."

facts.title: Grammy Awards Dominance (1968-1975)
facts.body: Aretha Franklin held the longest single-award Grammy streak in history, winning the prize for Best Female R&B Vocal Performance for eight consecutive years, from 1968 through 1975. This unparalleled achievement solidified her position as the premier artist of R&B during the early 1970s. "For the first 8 years that the Grammy Awards gave out a prize for best female R&B vocal performance, from 1968 through 1975, Aritha won that Grammy every year. facts.title: Birth Environment (c. 1968)
facts.body: Reggae emerged around 1968 in Jamaica, born out of a tumultuous period that saw the disillusionment of post-independence celebrations, rampant poverty in Kingston exacerbated by government bulldozing of squatter communities, and systemic political corruption that failed to address citizens' urgent needs for jobs. "It was in that environment that reggae was born around 1968."

facts.title: Decline of Original Era (c. 1968)
facts.body: The original Garage Rock era concluded around 1968, largely influenced by technological advancements in recording studios that led to more sophisticated recordings. Rock bands themselves became more refined in their live performances, songwriting, and overall presentation. The rise of the album format also contributed, as Garage Rock had primarily found success through 7-inch singles and struggled to adapt to albums, which became the preferred format with the shift from AM to FM radio. "The original garage rock era ended around 1968, largely because of technology."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Immigration Issues and Marijuana Conviction (1968/1972)
facts.body: John Lennon faced significant immigration challenges in the United States due to a marijuana conviction in England in 1968. This conviction was used by the US government as a reason to attempt his deportation, initiated in part by South Carolina Senator Strom Thurmond. This legal battle tied Lennon up in immigration court for a year and a half, preventing his planned anti-Nixon tour. "Lennon was not permitted into the country. He had a little bit of a problem with a previous arrest due to possession of marijuana."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s

facts.body: The second album by The Velvet Underground, released in 1968, exemplifies their raw and distorted sound. The track "Sister Ray" from this album was recorded in one take with no overdubs. Ron Kale contributed to the distorted sound by tuning an electric keyboard as low as it could go and then turning the volume as high as possible. Live performances of this track could extend for up to three-quarters of an hour, pushing every amp and instrument to its limits to create distortion and feedback. "Ron Kale uses an electric keyboard tuned down as low as it will go. And then, he turned up the volume as high as possible, which is how he got that distorted sound."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.body: The album, released in 1968, faced substantial censorship problems concerning both its original cover art and certain songs. These issues led to a five-month delay in its release, and it ultimately came out with a completely blank white cover featuring only the band's name and the album title, a direct consequence of the censorship. "el vegan zwankett que es el grandísimo album que saldría en 1968 tenía problemas de censura de la portada, tenía un problema de censura con las canciones... al final con cinco meses de retraso con una portada que como fue censurada quedó completamente en blanco solo con el nombre de los Rolling Stones y con el título del disco salía el grandísimo vegan zwankett."

facts.name: Beggars Banquet

facts.body: The release of *Beggar's Banquet* with a minimalist white cover, forced upon the band by censorship, coincidentally occurred at the same time as The Beatles' self-titled "White Album." This led to an unexpected parallel between the two major bands' album aesthetics, though The Rolling Stones' choice was involuntary. "volvía a tener problemas porque coincidía con el lanzamiento del guay de Albueno de los Beatles y ellos acaban de un album en blanco no porque quisieran que fuese blanco sino porque su portada había sido completamente censurada."

facts.title: Star-Spangled Banner Controversy (1968)
facts.body: At Game 5 of the World Series in Tiger Stadium, Detroit, Jose Feliciano performed a unique rendition of the Star-Spangled Banner in 1968, which was deemed "not traditional enough" by some, with Carlos Santana even calling it "too black." This performance caused significant backlash, leading American Legion clubs to call for a law dictating how the song should be sung, and Feliciano was controversially labeled a communist during the Cold War era. This event reportedly led to a period where he struggled to get radio play in America and had to perform in other countries, though sources debate if he was truly blacklisted, as he still secured a TV special in 1969 and played to packed houses. "I had to leave America and play in other countries because I wasn't getting any radio play after I did the Star Spangled Banner."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s

facts.name: José Feliciano

facts.title: Nike Commercial Controversy
facts.body: The original recording of "Revolution" was used in a highly controversial 1987 Nike commercial for their "Air Revolution" line of shoes. This use of what was considered "a sacred call to action" by John Lennon to sell shoes sparked immense public outrage. The ad agency, Wieden+Kennedy, chose the Beatles' song over an alternative by the Georgia Satellites. The licensing deal, worth between $7 and $10 million, was negotiated with Michael Jackson, who had acquired a significant portion of the Beatles' publishing catalog in 1985, and Yoko Ono, who supported the deal to expose her late husband's music to new generations. The remaining three Beatles (Paul, Ringo, and George) "went ballistic," suing Nike for $50 million, though the matter was settled out of court. The campaign significantly boosted Nike and became one of advertising's most influential spots, marking a turning point in commercial music licensing. "And what's more, this sacred call to action that John Lennon wrote in the 1960s was being used to sell shoes."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Concept of Selling Out: Part 1

facts.body: Featured on The Velvet Underground's 1968 album "White Light/White Heat," this song was recorded in a single take without overdubs. Its heavily distorted sound was achieved by Ron Kale tuning an electric keyboard to its lowest possible setting and then maximizing its volume. When performed live, the track could extend for up to three-quarters of an hour, with the band deliberately overdriving every amp and instrument to generate intense distortion and feedback. "The Velvet Underground and Sister Ray from 1968 creating distortion and feedback the old fashion way, over driving every amp and every instrument they had."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.name: Sister Ray

facts.body: Featured on The Velvet Underground's 1968 album "White Light/White Heat," this song was recorded in a single take without overdubs. Its heavily distorted sound was achieved by Ron Kale tuning an electric keyboard to its lowest possible setting and then maximizing its volume. When performed live, the track could extend for up to three-quarters of an hour, with the band deliberately overdriving every amp and instrument to generate intense distortion and feedback. "The Velvet Underground and Sister Ray from 1968 creating distortion and feedback the old fashion way, over driving every amp and every instrument they had."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Revival Single
facts.body: Released as the band's first new material after a period marked by low popularity and intense internal disputes, particularly between Keith Richards and Brian Jones. This single achieved immense success and signaled a powerful return to form for The Rolling Stones. "no esperan sacar un disco y simplemente sacan un primer material un primer sencillo, grandísimo Jean-Pin Jack Trash."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan

facts.title: Critical and Commercial Success
facts.body: This single achieved widespread success and was met with critical acclaim, with many critics declaring the return of the quintessential Rolling Stones sound. It marked a distinct departure from an awkward psychedelic phase and other commercial efforts that had diluted their core identity, successfully restoring the band to prominence. "tuvo muchísimo éxito la crítica decía que volvían los Rolling Stones de toda la vida y nuestros Rolling Stones que estaban un poco arregufo entre una psicodelia entre la que no se movían cómodos y un intento por ser comerciales que no lo había hecho perder su esencia y con el Jean-Pin Jack Trash vuelven un poco por todo lo alto tuvieron muchísimo éxito."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan

facts.title: Swift Production
facts.body: Following the success of the "Jumpin' Jack Flash" single, The Rolling Stones quickly entered the recording studio. Within just a few months, they completed this album, which would go on to be considered by many as potentially the best album of their career. "Se cerraron en el estudio de grabación y en menú unas pocos meses se acababan posiblemente el mejor disco de la carrera de los Rolling Stones."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: 1968: Cuando los Rolling Stones resucitaron
facts.name: Beggar's Banquet

facts.title: Censorship and Delayed Release
facts.body: The album, released in 1968, faced substantial censorship problems concerning both its original cover art and certain songs. These issues led to a five-month delay in its release, and it ultimately came out with a completely blank white cover featuring only the band's name and the album title, a direct consequence of the censorship. "el vegan zwankett que es el grandísimo album que saldría en 1968 tenía problemas de censura de la portada, tenía un problema de censura con las canciones... al final con cinco meses de retraso con una portada que como fue censurada quedó completamente en blanco solo con el nombre de los Rolling Stones y con el título del disco salía el grandísimo vegan zwankett."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: 1968: Cuando los Rolling Stones resucitaron
facts.name: Beggar's Banquet

facts.title: White Album Coincidence
facts.body: The release of *Beggar's Banquet* with a minimalist white cover, forced upon the band by censorship, coincidentally occurred at the same time as The Beatles' self-titled "White Album." This led to an unexpected parallel between the two major bands' album aesthetics, though The Rolling Stones' choice was involuntary. "volvía a tener problemas porque coincidía con el lanzamiento del guay de Albueno de los Beatles y ellos acaban de un album en blanco no porque quisieran que fuese blanco sino porque su portada había sido completamente censurada."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: 1968: Cuando los Rolling Stones resucitaron
facts.name: Beggar's Banquet

facts.title: Critical and Commercial Triumph
facts.body: Despite the initial challenges with production and censorship, *Beggar's Banquet* was met with overwhelming critical acclaim and promptly returned The Rolling Stones to the number one position, solidifying their status as "the greatest" band once more. "tenía unas enormes críticas volvían o traezan número uno volvían a ser los más grandes."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: 1968: Cuando los Rolling Stones resucitaron
facts.name: Beggar's Banquet

facts.body: Shatner's debut musical work was created in 1968 at the request of Decca Records. The album was conceptualized to link literature with music, with each six-minute cut comprising a three-minute piece of literature and a three-minute song. "You began recording musical works with a Transform Man in 1968."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Outsider Music
facts.name: The Transformed Man

facts.body: Shatner's vision for the album was to perform great speeches from literature, such as Shakespeare and Edmond Rostand, alongside contemporary song lyrics with melodic musical backgrounds. His aim was to illustrate either a comparative or an opposing philosophy between the literary and musical components of each track. "I'll do a literature, a piece of literature, and link it to music. Because I love literature and the great speeches that Shakespeare and Edmund Rostan wrote and all those people."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Outsider Music
facts.name: The Transformed Man

facts.body: The album was recorded in Los Angeles at a Decca studio. Shatner emphasized that for the album's concept to be understood, both the literary and musical parts of each six-minute cut had to be heard together, as taking one out of context would obscure his artistic intention. "Made in LA, if I remember correctly, to take a studio, some kind."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Outsider Music
facts.name: The Transformed Man

facts.body: This album was recorded after Decca Records asked Shatner to make a record while he was a young actor having success with Star Trek. He conceived it as a philosophical project linking classic literature (Shakespeare, Edmond Rostand) with modern song lyrics, aiming to show comparative or opposing philosophies. Each track was designed as a six-minute pairing (three minutes literature, three minutes music) meant to be heard together for context. "The most famous being the transformed man from 1968."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.body: Iron Butterfly was awarded the first Platinum Record for their album "In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida" in 1976. This award was introduced when the RIAA reformalized its sales certifications, with Platinum signifying sales of one million copies in the United States. "That was awarded to Iron Butterfly for Inagata De Vida."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.body: This hit single from "Disraeli Gears" achieved success by entering the Top 40 in early 1968, and later re-charting that summer to reach number five in August 1968. The song is notable for Jack Bruce's high tenor vocals, Eric Clapton's distinctive guitar riffs, and Ginger Baker's double bass drum work, offering "another glimpse of what is to come for heavy metal." Its structure, built around a repeated main riff, foreshadowed a common technique in heavy metal. Jack Bruce's lead vocal style on this track is also suggested as an influence on Robert Plant. "That made it into the top 40 in early 1968, then it was back on the charts again, that summer and made it to number five in August of 1968."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s
facts.episode: Ep. 24 - Loud, Louder, Loudest - 70s Heavy Metal
facts.name: Sunshine of Your Love

facts.title: First Proper Public Performance (March 1968)
facts.body: The band's first official public performance took place in March 1968. The opening act for this show was unusual: a food processor (blender with water) roaring through the PA system for about 15 minutes. "The first proper public performance came in March of 1968. The opening act for this show was a food processor."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 1
facts.name: The Psychedelic Stooges

facts.body: This song was written by George Harrison around the same time that Led Zeppelin's "Babe, I'm Gonna Leave You" was conceived, both featuring a similar guitar riff but with different tempos. "Which by the way was conceived around the same time that George Harrison wrote while my guitar gently weeps for the Beatles. Same riff, but different tempo."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
